claim: plaintiff contractor's claims to payment certificates for the value of the remedial and protective works ordered
requested_remedy: plaintiff contractor's claims to payment certificates for the value of the remedial and protective works ordered

facts.F1: The plaintiff company undertook to construct a railway tunnel through Beacon Hill with a view to providing double tracking for the Kowloon-Canton Railway by a PWD contract No. 413 of 1977 dated 20th December, 1977.
facts.F2: The construction was to be completed in about 2 1/2 years, and the whole project would involve over $78,000,000.
facts.F3: The PWD contract incorporated the standard Conditions of Contract for Civil Engineering Construction (1971 edition) which is taken from the I.C.E. General Conditions of Contract.
facts.F4: After the commencement of work on the 3rd January, 1978, six water mains were located near the North Portal to the tunnel some three metres below ground level.
facts.F5: Subsidence was detected, and the safety of these water mains responsible for the supply of all the drinking water for Kowloon was threatened.
facts.F6: In November, 1978, work stopped so as to avoid causing further deflection of these water mains.
facts.F7: Differences arose between the Engineer and the plaintiff contractor.
facts.F8: Remedial and protective measures were designed, and between the 29th November, 1978 to the 17th March, 1979, six written instructions were issued by the Engineer to the plaintiff contractor.
facts.F9: The works so ordered by the Engineer took several months to complete and allegedly incurred some $20,000,000.
facts.F10: By a letter to the Engineer dated the 30th March, 1979, the plaintiff contractor referred the liability for and quantum of these remedial and protective works to the Engineer for his decision.
facts.F11: On the 24th March, 1980, the Engineer gave his decision, whereby most of the plaintiff contractor's claims to payment certificates for the value of the remedial and protective works ordered were rejected.
facts.F12: The plaintiff contractor had persisted in including the value of these works in the monthly payment applications, but the Engineer had continued to exclude these items from the payment certificates.
facts.F13: Being dissatisfied with the Engineer's decision, by a letter dated the 6th June, 1980 the plaintiff contractor required the Director of Public Works to refer the dispute to arbitration.
facts.F14: Government refused to give its consent to arbitrate before the completion of the entire PWD contract.
facts.F15: There was a case of A.E. Farr Limited v. The Ministry of Transport, where Buckley, J. emphasized that interim certificates were subject to final adjustments in the usual provisions of the I.C.E. General Conditions of Contract.
facts.F16: There was a case of F.R. Absalom Limited v. The Great Western (London) Garden Village Society, where the question of withholding a certificate was never directly in issue.
facts.F17: There were criticisms made in Hudson's Building and Engineering Contracts 10th Edition regarding certifying works.
facts.F18: There was a genuine dispute as to whether payment and thus a certificate is due for works executed.

lawsuit_type: judicial interpretation of Clause 120(6) and consequential declarations
reference_issues: Whether the plaintiff contractor is entitled to have the matter arbitrated as of now without the written consent of Government prior to the completion of the PWD contract

facts.F1: The applicant was the tenant of the domestic premises at 26G Shouson Hill Road, Hong Kong, under a tenancy agreement dated 24 February 1977.
facts.F2: The initial tenancy was for 3 years from 1 March 1977 at a calendar monthly rent of $8,500 exclusive of rates.
facts.F3: The tenancy was extended for 2 years from 1 June 1980 at an increased calendar monthly rent of $10,285 exclusive of rates.
facts.F4: The rateable value of the suit premises is $96,000.
facts.F5: The applicant applied for a new tenancy under Section 117 of the Landlord and Tenant (Consolidation) Ordinance, Cap. 7.
facts.F6: The respondent does not object to the grant of a new tenancy but the parties disagree on the duration and rent of the new tenancy.
facts.F7: The applicant seeks a new tenancy of 9 months duration or alternatively a 2-year duration.
facts.F8: The respondent offers a 2-year term.
facts.F9: The Tribunal determines that the duration of the new tenancy shall be for a period of 2 years.
facts.F10: The applicant submits that the new tenancy should commence on 1 October 1982.
facts.F11: The respondent submits that the new tenancy should commence on 1 July 1982.
facts.F12: The Tribunal orders that the 2-year duration of the new tenancy shall commence on 1 July 1982.
facts.F13: The applicant and respondent submit valuations for the fair market rent of the premises.
facts.F14: The applicant's valuer, Mr. Cheung, assesses the rent at $29,500 per calendar month exclusive of rates for a 2-year lease from 22 September 1982.
facts.F15: The respondent's valuer, Mr. Lui, assesses the rent at $40,000 per calendar month exclusive of rates for a 2-year lease from 1 July 1982.
facts.F16: The valuers use different total gross floor areas in their valuations.
facts.F17: The applicant's valuer calculates the gross area as 224.08 square meters (2,412 square feet).
facts.F18: The respondent's valuer calculates the gross area as 298.77 square meters (3,216 square feet).
facts.F19: The difference in valuations arises from the inclusion of an enclosed foundation area used as a playroom in the respondent's valuation.
facts.F20: The Tribunal holds that the lawful residential user of the property is restricted to the 3 stories comprising the upper, middle, and lower levels.
facts.F21: The enclosed foundation area does not form part of the legal gross floor area but is part of the suit premises and must be taken into account for valuation purposes.
facts.F22: The garden and carpark areas are also ancillary facilities that must be taken into account.
facts.F23: The valuers did not make sufficient allowance for the relatively inferior car parking facilities.
facts.F24: Springfield Gardens is a comparable property with a rent of $35,000 per calendar month exclusive of rates.

reference_issues: Determination of the duration of the new tenancy
Determination of the fair market rent of the premises

facts.F1: On 25 January 1997, a fire was deliberately started in Top One Karaoke on the 2nd to 4th floors of Fung Lee Commercial Building at 6-8A, Prat Avenue, Tsimshatsui, resulting in 17 fatalities and 13 injuries.
facts.F2: The fire started around 3 a.m. with the use of 'molotov' cocktails, likely involving persons with triad links.
facts.F3: The fire was not accidental, but rather the result of arson.
facts.F4: The premises were owned by the 1st Defendant, managed by the 2nd Defendant, and leased to the 3rd Defendant.
facts.F5: The common areas, including stairways, landings, and lobby areas, were fitted out with combustible materials, such as polyurethane foam filled sofas, wood panelling, and synthetic materials.
facts.F6: The 4th Defendant was responsible for the installation and maintenance of the sprinkler system and fire protection equipment.
facts.F7: The Fire Services Investigation found that the sprinkler system failed to function due to closed gate valves, and other fire prevention measures were lacking.
facts.F8: The defendants failed to ensure the existence of proper maintenance and inspection to ensure safety and an administrative section to deal with fire risk and prevention.
facts.F9: The closure of the gate valves, lack of access panels, and failure to check and maintain the sprinkler system were all contributing factors to the fire and resulting deaths
facts.F10: Simple and achievable measures could have been taken by the defendants to prevent the risk of fire.

Whether the 1st and 2nd Defendants were responsible for the maintenance of the common areas, including stairways, landings, and lobby areas
Whether the 4th Defendant was responsible for ensuring the proper functioning of the sprinkler system

facts.F10: The Applicant's father, mother, and siblings died as a result of the supposed charm.
facts.F11: The Applicant himself started to have haematuria (blood in urine) and the doctor diagnosed that was the result of poisoning.
facts.F12: In 2005, he moved to live with his father's close friend, Ugwu, in another area of Nigeria.
facts.F13: In late 2008, he decided to leave Nigeria and went to Guinea for the first time and obtained his Guinean passport and a visa for China.
facts.F14: He returned to Nigeria in around April 2009 and departed Nigeria for China in May 2009.
facts.F15: He stayed in the Mainland for a few days before he arrived in Hong Kong with his Guinean passport.
facts.F16: The Director rejected the Applicant's non-refoulement claim on all applicable grounds by notices of decision dated 7 June 2016 and 8 December 2016 respectively.

facts.F19: No appeal was made to the Board in respect of the second decision of the Director.
facts.F20: The Applicant filed a Form 86 on 31 May 2018 for leave to apply for judicial review of the decision of the Board and the first decision of the Director.
facts.F21: The Applicant's claim of poor health and problem with writing was made without any documentary evidence in support.

facts.F23: The Applicant has the option of re-settling in Guinea.
facts.F24: Internal relocation is a viable option for him in Nigeria.

facts.F3: He was arrested by police on 2 January 2014 and referred to the Immigration Department for investigation.
facts.F4: He raised a non-refoulement claim on the basis that if he returned to Vietnam he would be harmed or killed by his creditor for failing to repay his loan and that he would also be sued by the bank over the default of his loan and/or by his customers for failing to deliver their goods after he had suffered a traffic accident.
facts.F5: The Applicant was released on recognizance pending the determination of his claim.
facts.F6: In 2010, he mortgaged his home to a bank for a loan for purchasing a vehicle to start a transportation business, but in January 2013, he had a traffic accident and his vehicle was a total loss without insurance.
facts.F7: He was unable to work to repay the bank or the money-lender, and as a result, his house was possessed by the bank, which also sued him for the balance of his loan.
facts.F8: His customers also sued him for failing to deliver their goods, while the money-lender had sent men to threaten and beat him up over his failure to repay his loan.
facts.F9: To avoid such threats and law suits, the Applicant fled to hide in his uncle’s place in Hau Loc District and eventually departed Vietnam on 27 December 2013 for China and then for Hong Kong.
facts.F10: Upon his arrest, he raised his non-refoulement claim for protection, for which he completed a Non-refoulement Claim Form (“NCF”) on 6 August 2016.
facts.F11: He attended a screening interview before the Immigration Department with legal representation from the Duty Lawyer Service (“DLS”).
facts.F12: By a Notice of Decision dated 8 September 2016, the Director of Immigration (“Director”) rejected the Applicant’s claim on all then applicable grounds, including risk of torture under Part VIIC of the Immigration Ordinance, Cap 115 (“Torture Risk”), risk of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment under Article 3 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance, Cap 383 (“HKBOR”) (“BOR 3 Risk”), and risk of persecution with reference to the non-refoulement principle under Article 33 of the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (“Persecution Risk”).

facts.F15: On 1 August 2018, the Applicant filed his Form 86 for leave to apply for judicial review of the Board’s decision.
facts.F16: The court found a delay of more than 2 months to be significant or substantial in the context of filing an application for leave to apply for judicial review.
facts.F17: The court found that the Applicant had failed to present a proper challenge to the decisions of the Director and the Board.
